newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Stream of voters swells in Moroccan referendum.
newsitem.headline: Stream of voters swells in Moroccan referendum.

text.p: Moroccans went to the polls on Friday to vote in a referendum to change the nation's constitution and set up a second house of parliament, moves seen as a way to decentralise power and help rural development.

King Hassan, pro-government and the main opposition parties have called for people to vote in favour of the referendum and officials expect an overwhelming endorsement for a second house with power to force a no-confidence vote in the government.

Officials see indirect elections to the second house, elected mainly through local councils, professional bodies and trade unions, as a means of spreading political influence to areas of the country that have had little say in political decisions.

The proposed changes to the 1992 constitution are also widely seen as a way to help development in rural areas, home to 50 percent of the country's 27 million people, and a major contributor through farm products to foreign currency earnings.
King Hassan's paramount powers will not be touched.

At Moulay Youssef high school, near the royal palace in central Rabat, officials in two booths said that by 11 a.m. (1100 GMT) the number of voters was up by as much as 50 percent on a 1992 referendum to reinforce the prime minister's powers and introduce human rights reforms.
One young woman, who cast ballots for herself and her husband, said: "I voted "yes" because this is what my head told me."
At another school, Lycee Hassan II, one official said voting was up by about one-third on the last referendum.
"I voted today to respond to King Hassan's appeal," said Khadija al-Idrissi, a 42-year-old housewife.
In Casablanca, the main financial city, eyewitnesses reported a steady stream of voters, mainly women casting their ballots as they did their morning shopping.

The official news agency MAP said that by 10 a.m. (1000 GMT) 30 percent of registered voters in Oujda Angad near the Algerian border had cast their votes, while the lowest turnout, five percent, was in the northern city of Tangier.
White banners bearing the legend in Arabic "Referendum, 13 September" fluttered in sunshine outside booths as they opened in Rabat.

Some 12 million Moroccans are eligible to vote, including more than 118,000 people in the disputed Western Sahara. Voting is due to end at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT) with final results late on Friday and a final tally on Saturday.

"It's an historic moment for this country. For the first time there is a general consensus, including the opposition, to vote 'Yes' for the proposals," said one senior official on the eve of the vote.
The lower house, now with one-third of its members elected indirectly, will be elected directly, a demand long made by opposition parties.
